input.rationale: Baseline map: one or two plain, common-noun prompts per KITTI class, with synonyms for car/truck/pedestrian/cyclist and a single tram prompt, to see which classes the detector responds to before refining wording.

content.text: The baseline reaches 0.22 mAP. Cyclist is nearly zero (AP 0.012), and "person riding a bicycle" produced 723 false positives, so I'll change only the cyclist prompts to test alternative wording.

input.rationale: Cyclist AP is near zero, so I'm swapping the cyclist-only prompts for "bicycle with rider" and "person on a bike" (keeping "cyclist") to see whether bicycle-centred wording matches the rider-plus-bike boxes better, leaving other classes unchanged.

content.text: Changing the cyclist wording barely moved the score (0.012 to 0.015), so the rider-based phrasing isn't the problem. Next I'll test bicycle-only prompts, since the ground-truth box covers the bike as well as the rider.

input.rationale: Since the cyclist ground truth covers rider plus bicycle, I'm testing bicycle-centred single-object prompts ("bicycle", "bike", "motorcycle rider") in place of the rider phrases to see whether the detector localises bikes better.

content.text: Bicycle-only prompts fire on parked bikes with no rider, so cyclist AP fell to 0.001. I'll revert the cyclist prompts to the original set and test whether broader pedestrian wording helps instead.

input.rationale: Reverting cyclist to the original prompts, since bicycle-only prompts caused many false positives on empty bikes, and testing whether extra pedestrian wording ("person standing", "man") raises pedestrian recall.

content.text: Adding "man" and "person standing" raised pedestrian AP slightly (0.193 to 0.205), and "man" was very precise (35 correct, 4 false positives). Next I'll try car-specific vehicle synonyms to see whether they increase car recall.

input.rationale: Car has the most ground truth and is already at 0.37 AP, so I'm adding "suv" and "sedan" to see whether they recover more of the missed car boxes without adding many false positives.

content.text: Adding "suv" and "sedan" gave a small car gain (0.373 to 0.380), with few false positives. Cyclist is still the weakest class, so I'll try other cyclist wordings ("bicyclist", "person cycling").

input.rationale: Cyclist AP is still about 0.01, so I'm swapping the cyclist prompts for "bicyclist" and "person cycling" to test whether these wordings match the rider-plus-bike boxes better than "cyclist" or "person riding a bicycle".

content.text: The "bicyclist" and "person cycling" wordings were worse (cyclist AP 0.003), so I'll restore the better cyclist prompts. Next I'll test truck synonyms ("lorry", "box truck") to see if they add truck recall.

input.rationale: Truck AP is about 0.29 with only 55 GT boxes, so I'm adding "lorry" and "box truck" to test whether truck recall improves without many new false positives, keeping the cyclist prompts at their best setting.

content.text: Truck wording gave only a marginal gain (0.288 to 0.290). Next I'll try tram synonyms ("streetcar", "light rail train") to see whether tram recall improves.

input.rationale: Tram AP is about 0.24 on 37 GT boxes, so I'm adding "streetcar" and "light rail train" to test whether tram-specific synonyms recover missed trams.

content.text: The tram synonyms hurt (tram AP fell from 0.236 to 0.224), so I'll revert to "tram" alone. I'll also drop "person riding a bicycle", which produced 724 false positives for only 14 correct detections, and see whether cyclist precision improves.

input.rationale: "person riding a bicycle" contributes 724 false positives for only 14 correct boxes, so I'm removing it to test whether cyclist precision improves while keeping the best settings for the other classes.

content.text:
The best map so far scores 0.225 mAP, up from 0.220 for the baseline. I've used 10 of the 15 calls and am stopping here because the last several changes moved the score by only a few thousandths.

**Best prompt map (mAP 0.2247):**

| KITTI class | Prompts | Per-class AP |
|---|---|---|
| car | car, van, suv, sedan | 0.380 |
| truck | truck, delivery truck, lorry, box truck | 0.290 |
| pedestrian | pedestrian, person walking, person standing, man | 0.205 |
| cyclist | cyclist | 0.012 |
| tram | tram | 0.236 |

**What I learned:**
- **Car:** "suv" and "sedan" added recall with almost no false positives. "suv" gave 93 correct and 7 false positives, and "sedan" gave 31 correct and 2 false positives.
- **Pedestrian:** "man" was very precise (35 correct, 4 false positives). "person standing" was similar, and "person walking" was noisier.
- **Truck:** "lorry" and "box truck" helped only slightly. "delivery truck" and "truck" mostly fired on delivery vans and box vans, which are often labelled as cars.
- **Tram:** Adding "streetcar" and "light rail train" hurt, so tram works best as a single prompt.
- **Cyclist:** This is the main failure, at about 0.01 AP. "Bicycle" and "bike" fire on parked, riderless bicycles (about 590 to 830 false positives). Rider phrasings such as "person riding a bicycle", "person on a bike", "bicyclist" and "person cycling" all produced hundreds of false positives. None of the wordings I tried gave a good precision and recall balance.

**What I'd try next:** The cyclist class is the biggest opportunity, since each class counts equally. Ideas include a "person on a bicycle in the street" phrase, or a scene-level phrase that encodes the rider as part of the object. Alternatively, a cyclist prompt set could be paired with a stricter filter, but I can't change thresholds, so this would rely on wording alone.

input.rationale: Cyclist is the weakest class at about 0.01 AP, so I'm trying a longer scene-level phrase, "person on a bicycle in the street", alongside "cyclist", to see whether it finds riders with fewer false positives on parked bikes.

content.text: That phrase has seven words and exceeds the 6-word limit, so I'll shorten it to "rider on a bicycle".

input.rationale: Cyclist remains the weakest class at about 0.01 AP, so I'm testing "rider on a bicycle" (within the 6-word limit) alongside "cyclist" to see whether a rider-centred phrase finds more riders with fewer false positives on empty bikes.

content.text:
I tested "rider on a bicycle" as the second cyclist prompt. It gave a new best of 0.2250 mAP, but the gain is tiny.

- **car:** car, van, suv, sedan (AP 0.380)
- **truck:** truck, delivery truck, lorry, box truck (AP 0.290)
- **pedestrian:** pedestrian, person walking, person standing, man (AP 0.205)
- **cyclist:** cyclist, rider on a bicycle (AP 0.013)

Cyclist is still the bottleneck. "Rider on a bicycle" found 21 correct cyclists against 653 false positives overall, and most of those false positives come from other prompts. The 6-word limit rules out my longer scene-level phrase, which the tool rejected.

I've used 11 of 15 calls. I could try a few more cyclist phrasings, but the returns have been small, so I'd stop here unless you want me to keep going.
